newsitem.title: UK: Metal traders eye Zaire but see no present impact.
newsitem.headline: Metal traders eye Zaire but see no present impact.

text.p: London metals traders on Wednesday kept an eye on news from Zaire where aid workers feared strife in a part of the country after authorities gave 200,000 ethnic Tutsis a week to leave.

But they said there was no impact on prices either for copper on the London Metal Exchange (LME) or for free-market cobalt, Zaire's two important mineral exports. Traders said details were always welcome on any political developments in Zaire but metal exports did not move through any of the areas that seemed likely to suffer in any flare-up.

The key mining area around Lubumbashi is well to the south of the Burundi/Rwanda borders and the zone of tension. "There is always a flurry of interest on trouble in Zaire in the cobalt market," a minor metals trader said. Zaire's state-owned mining company Gecamines in recent years has concentrated more on cobalt than copper, with output of both metals well below the heights of the mid-1980s, traders noted.
Gecamines officials in London were not immediately available for comment.

Copper's current supply/demand picture is finely balanced with stock levels low. Supply disruptions, however small, would bolster the price, an analyst said. Zaire's cobalt production this year is likely to be 5,000-5,500 tonnes against 4,400 tonnes in 1995.
In copper, industry specialists Bloomsbury Minerals Economics said Zaire production last year was 35,000 tonnes.
Production of both copper and cobalt has slumped from the high levels of 470,000 tonnes and 17,000 tonnes in the 1980s.
At the lows cobalt output was just 2,000 tonnes in 1993 and in 1994 copper production bottomed out at 30,000.
On the LME copper was trading around $1,920 a tonne against $1,949 on Tuesday. High grade cobalt was indicated at a steady $22.75/23.50/lb.
